This is the best-sourced case I have seen from this team and it fails anyway, which is the lesson worth more than the pitch. Every figure I pulled from the FY2025 10-K and Q2'26 10-Q reproduced exactly. The research is real. The case still dies, for three independent reasons, any one of which is sufficient.

FIRST, IT CONTRADICTS ITSELF. The whole valuation is one parameter — 44.5% incremental drop-through — and the case's own FY26 build implies 31.2% for the next two quarters. It never notices. Carry its own forward-implied number into 2027 and Power EBITDA lands at $5,335M versus Street's $5,600M. The long inverts into a short versus consensus without changing a single input the case did not itself supply.

SECOND, THE 10-K HANDS GLJ THE WIN. Three lines below the Power EBITDA table the case quotes, the FY2025 10-K discloses FY25 Power revenue +10% organically and EBITDA +18% organically — a 22.5% organic drop-through. GLJ's implied 2027 figure is 21.8%. The case's own sensitivity says halving to 22.25% means the long is "gone, not damaged." It then declares the downside case "reachable" and the upside case not. It is correct on both counts and argues the long anyway. Selecting the reported 38.7% over the organic 22.5% off the same page, silently, is the kind of thing that ends a pitch in the room.

THIRD, THERE IS NOTHING LEFT TO WIN. 79.5% of the GLJ move reversed by Sep 18 — $16.94 of residual, 1.8%. The case's own Street-relative edge is $19.34, 2.06%. And 91% of the $214 target upside is a re-rate from the 20.2x the market already pays on the case's own 2028E to 25x, with zero dependence on the backlog-vintage argument that is the entire thesis. Holding today's multiple returns spot to the cent. A PM will ask what he is buying that is not a multiple call, and the answer is $19.

WHAT TO KEEP. Two pieces of this work are genuinely load-bearing and should migrate into whatever the team pitches. (1) The POC/SRA mechanism is correct and well-evidenced: equipment revenue is recognized on cost-to-cost, an SRA holds a slot and not a price, and 34 GW converted at 2025-26 pricing with H1'26 orders priced >20% above 4Q'25. That is a real structural insight about how price enters the P&L. (2) The observation that only ~29% of GLJ's $2.03B EBITDA gap is the vintage argument at all, leaving 71% unexplained, is the right way to attack a bear note — and it points at the question the team should actually be researching.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD. The drop-through dispersion this exercise uncovered — 22% to 54% across six company disclosures in eighteen months — is itself the finding. It says the single number that sets GEV's 2027 earnings is not knowable from public filings to better than a factor of two, on a stock at 35x forward earnings whose January call will print both the 2027 outlook and the 2026 backlog-margin change. That is an argument about uncertainty being mispriced, not about direction, and it is more honest than either side of the current debate. If the team must pick a direction by Friday, note that the prior run's technical sweep already landed lean-LONG 55/45 on other grounds — this case adds nothing to that and should not be cited as support for it.

One process note for the team: the case's data_gaps section is excellent and flags the GLJ-model opacity, the unit-definition ambiguity and the corpus dating defect honestly. Keep writing those. But a gap list does not rescue a thesis whose central parameter the author's own source contradicts — and the $75/share headline should never have been computed against a $470 outlier's model rather than against the price. Measure edge against the market, always.

## [Redteam] attack2:L_fleet_services_wave

- **survives**: False
- **arithmetic_checks_out**: False
- **arithmetic_errors**: Four arithmetic/logical failures, in order of severity.

(1) THE SIGNATURE STATISTIC IS AN ARTIFACT, NOT A SIGNAL. The case's headline — "14.2% of lifetime major-parts events completed against 24.4% of lifetime fired hours" — is presented as proof of a deferred annuity. I reproduced it and then asked what a fleet with NO wave would show. Take the case's own lifetime ladder (126,000 h; HGP@25k w=1, MI@50k w=2, HGP@75k w=1, MI@100k w=2, HGP@125k w=1; total weight 7) and a perfectly steady-state fleet uniformly distributed over its lifetime hours. Exact integral: mean event fraction = 40.48%, mean hours fraction = 50.00%. Gap = 9.52 points. The case's measured gap is 24.4 − 14.3 = 10.1 points. A fleet in perfect equilibrium with zero wave produces the same gap the case treats as its central evidence. The statistic is a step-function artifact: events sit at the END of each interval, so the event fraction always lags the hours fraction. It is also non-monotone in the thing the case cares about — at h=49,999 the gap is 25.4 points (biggest "wave ahead") when the unit is one hour from its major; at h=50,001 the gap is −3.2 points. A metric that swings 28 points across one operating hour measures nothing about timing. Pillar 2's claim sentence is falsified by its own arithmetic.

(2) THE DOLLARS ARE UNIT COUNT, NOT THE WAVE — AND THE CASE SAYS SO. I decomposed Pillar 1's +$0.72B myself. 2025 implied yield factor = $1.01B/(126 × $10.0M) = 0.802. Unit-count effect at constant yield = (189−126) × $10M × 0.802 = $505M (70%). Yield effect on units already running = 126 × $10M × (0.914−0.802) = $142M (20%). Cross term $71M. Total $717M, ties. So 80% of Pillar 1 is new commissioning — the equipment backlog every model on the street already carries — and only $142M of revenue is the actual outage-wave mechanism. At the case's own 30% margin that is $43M EBITDA = $0.160/share × 25x = $4.00/share = 0.43% of $940.33. The thesis sentence is about outage timing; the dollars are about shipping more turbines. That is a bait-and-switch, and the case's own effect_on_model paragraph concedes the split ("+$144M yield, +$576M new commissioning") without carrying it into the headline.

(3) E = 0.625 IS A ZERO-DEGREE-OF-FREEDOM FIT SOLD AS A CONFIRMATION. Pillar 2's claim says the reconciliation works "with no fitted parameters." Its own fifth evidence item then says: "Solving (1−E) + E×0.68 = 0.80 gives E = 0.625." One equation, one unknown, one observation. It cannot fail, so it confirms nothing. Worse, the observation it is fitted to is not stable: Strazik's own words on the Sep-2026 tape are "a little bit more than $1 billion," and the deck says "~$1B." At $1.15B the realized yield is $9.13M/unit = 91% of steady state, not 80%, and E solves to roughly 0.28 instead of 0.625. The entire fitted billing split is absorbing the rounding in a one-significant-figure number management rounded itself.

(4) DOUBLE-COUNTING AND A FALSE CROSS-CHECK. Pillar 3 (Power services +9% vs +6%) overlaps Pillar 1 entirely: HA services ($1B) sits inside Power services (FY25 $13,072M, verified from XBRL OperatingSegments;Service;PowerSegment). Adding $216M and $100M counts the same revenue twice. Separately, Pillar 3's "29% complete on costs vs my 24.4% of HA lifetime hours — two independent measures agreeing within 5 points" is not a cross-check: the 29% is the whole LTSA book, ~1,800 gas turbines across every frame and vintage, overwhelmingly not HA. Two different populations agreeing to 5 points is coincidence dressed as corroboration.

Minor: FY24→FY25 Power services is +5.5% (12,391 → 13,072), not the +5.9% quoted. The 25x is applied pre-tax to an EBITDA delta with no tax bridge; at ~24% the equity-equivalent multiple is ~19x.
- **evidence_holds**: False
- **evidence_problems**: The SOURCING is unusually clean — almost every quoted fact reproduces. What fails is what the facts are made to mean.

VERIFIED, exactly as stated: the installed-base panel (8-K/EX 2024-03-08 "92 HA-Turbines in the installed base with over two million operating hours"; 10-Q 2024-04-30 "94"; 424B3 2024-07-24 "100"; 424B3 2024-10-23 "106"; Dec-24 "115"; 10-K 2026-01-29 "51 HA-Turbines in RPO, 43 being installed and commissioned, and 126 HA-Turbines in our installed base"). The Dec-2025 deck slide (gev_webcast_presentation_12092025.pdf): "Installed HA units ~125 → ~400 … HA services annual revenue (~$1B in 2025) expected to reach ~$4B by '35." The CSA revision figures (10-K 2026-01-29 "net unfavorable changes in estimated profitability of $151 million"; FY24 $319M; H1'26 $218M; Q1'24 $29M). Power services revenue series. The Strazik Sep-18 quotes. All real.

Now the three places the evidence turns against the case.

(a) THE DECK ATTRIBUTES ITS OWN $1B→$4B TO SOMETHING ELSE. Directly under the numbers the case quotes, the same slide says the driver is "Strong escalation on existing contracts and price on new contracts." Do the arithmetic: units 125→400 is 3.20x, revenue 1→4 is 4.00x, so implied yield rises 1.250x over ten years = 2.26% a year. That is ordinary contractual escalation. Management's own slide fully accounts for the $8.0M→$10.0M yield gap with price, leaving nothing for an outage wave to explain. The case takes its primary source's headline numbers and discards that source's stated mechanism without saying so.

(b) THE MECHANISM HAS ALREADY BEEN TESTED IN-SAMPLE AND PRINTED ZERO. Pillar 3's claim is that CSA revenue "must inflect with the event count." The case's own cohort model puts events at 20 (2024) → 30 (2025) → 39 (2026): +95% over two years. Over that exact window CSA revenues recognized went $5,473M (FY24) → $5,412M (FY25) → $2,689M H1'26 (×2 = $5,378M). Down 1.7%. Fleet hours roughly doubled (2.0M → 4.0M) and units went 92 → 130 over the same stretch. The one line the case says is mechanically chained to the outage count has been flat-to-down through a near-doubling of the outage count. The elasticity the whole case requires has already been measured, and it is approximately zero.

(c) THE COHORT CURVE IS FITTED WHEN OBSERVED DATA EXISTS. The case says (weakest_link 4) it has no unit-level series. But GEV discloses HA-Turbine SALES in units every year in the Power unit table: 2021: 13, 2022: 11, 2023: 14, 2024: 15, 2025: 24, H1'26: 8 (10-K 2026-01-29, 10-K 2025-02-06, 8-K/EX 2024-03-08, 10-Q 2026-07-22). That is an available constraint the case never used. It happens to be roughly consistent with the fitted 2021-23 numbers, so this is not fatal — but declaring a variable unobservable when the filings publish it is a research failure, and it means the "one curve of three tested" defence rests on a search the analyst did not finish.

(d) The case ignores combustion inspections entirely. CIs are the frequent, smaller event class and the fleet has been doing them throughout. Counting only HGP/MI events maximises the measured "deficit." The choice of which events to count is doing load-bearing work that is never disclosed.

(e) The 6,300 h/unit/yr spine is not precise to ±3% as claimed. All three "independent" derivations draw on the same anchors rounded to one decimal place. On the cleanest window (Dec-24 "approximately 2.9M" → Dec-25 "approximately 3.6M", 120.5 unit-years) the rounding band alone spans 4,979 to 6,639 h/yr, centre 5,809 — below the case's 6,300. Dec-23's anchor is "over two million," a floor, not a point.

You cannot pitch as a variant view something a bulge bracket published eleven days ago and the tape already moved on.

2. THE CASE'S OWN "THIRD DATED TEST" IS ALREADY PUBLIC ON THE PRICING DATE. The case says what would matter is "Strazik's new number: ~$100B of contracted future HA services revenue by end-2027." That number is in the Yahoo/MarketBeat article dated 2026-09-18 — the $940.33 close — which the case cites for a different quote in the same paragraph: "By the end of next year, he said, GE Vernova expects to have contracted about $100 billion in future HA services revenue." The catalyst the case is waiting for happened before the price it is measuring against. It is in the $940.33.

3. THE DECEMBER 2025 INVESTOR DECK IS THE PRIMARY SOURCE FOR TWO OF THREE PILLARS. Slide 28 has been public for nine months, moved the stock +15.6% on 3.75x volume the next day, and fully reversed within five sessions. The market saw the $1B→$4B HA services annuity slide, repriced it, and gave the repricing back. Building a long on a nine-month-old deck slide that the market already round-tripped is the definition of a known fact.

4. THE UNIT-COUNT COMPONENT — 70% of Pillar 1's dollars — is the 116 GW under contract, the 20→24→30 GW/yr output ramp, and the $176B RPO. That is the single most covered fact about this company. GEV trades at ~35x forward against an S&P at ~22x precisely because the street models it.

What is genuinely NOT priced is the opposite trade. GLJ initiated Sell at $470 on Sep 14 on 2027 equipment margin; Bernstein went cautious Sep 18. The debated variable is margin on the equipment vintage, not the existence of a services annuity. This case answers a question nobody is asking.
- **killer_question**: "Your own cohort model has the HA outage count going from 20 events in 2024 to 30 in 2025 to 39 in 2026 — a 95% increase — and your Pillar 3 says contractual-services revenue is mechanically chained to that count through cost-to-cost percentage-of-completion. Over that exact window GEV's filed CSA revenue recognized went $5,473M to $5,412M to $5,378M annualized. It fell. So the elasticity you need has already been measured out-of-model, in the filings, on the only two years where both the event count and the revenue line are observable, and it printed zero. What number do you have that tells me 43 events in 2027 will do something 39 events in 2026 did not — other than the fact that you have run out of past?"

The follow-up he asks before you finish answering: "And separately — I ran your event-versus-hours statistic on a fleet in perfect steady state with no wave at all. It shows a 9.5-point gap. You measured 10.1. Explain to me what your headline number distinguishes."
- **revised_dollars_per_share**: +$4.00/share (+0.43% of $940.33), implied target $944. Round it to zero.

DERIVATION, line by line.

PILLAR 1 — keep only the part that is actually the thesis.
  2025 implied yield factor = $1.01B ÷ (126 units × $10.0M) = 0.802.
  Yield ("wave") effect on units already running at YE-25 = 126 × $10.0M × (0.914 − 0.802) = $142M revenue.
  Unit-count effect $505M + cross term $71M = $576M: ZEROED. That is the shipment ramp; it is in consensus, it is why the stock is at 35x, and it is not the outage-wave thesis.
  $142M × 30% incremental margin (the case's own, unsourced, assumption — kept for argument) = $42.6M EBITDA.
  $42,600,000 ÷ 266,333,581 = $0.160/share.
  $0.160 × 25x = $4.00/share = 0.43% of $940.33.

PILLAR 2 — ZEROED, and it should probably be negative.
  "Reversion to the ten-quarter mean" has no mechanism attached. As a percentage of contract revenue the series is FY24 5.83%, FY25 2.79%, H1'26 8.11% — H1'26 is the worst in the series, not a deviation due to snap back. And the case's own weakest_link 2 documents the 7HA.02 fleet-leader major (unit past 48,000 hours): stage-1 bucket TBC spallation, through-wall holes in leading-edge regions, deformed stator vane ring joint keys, ~75 TILs on the platform, 40 of 64 attendees grading GEV C or below with "desperation for spare parts." If the first majors land above estimate, the identical event schedule that powers Pillar 1 powers MORE unfavorable revisions, not fewer. The case cannot claim the outages are a revenue tailwind and a margin tailwind from the same physics while conceding it cannot resolve the sign. A PM books that as a risk, not a credit. Honest range: −$200M to +$161M, centred below zero.

PILLAR 3 — ZEROED twice over. It double-counts Pillar 1 (HA services sits inside Power services), and "if FY27 grows 9% instead of 6%" has no source. It is an assumption typed into a spreadsheet.

TOTAL: $42.6M EBITDA → $0.160/share → $4.00/share at 25x → target $944.
After a ~24% tax bridge, if you are benchmarking to an earnings multiple rather than EV/EBITDA: $3.04/share (0.32%).

IN-HORIZON (3–12 months, which is the assignment). The case's own model steps events 39 (2026) → 43 (2027): +10% on a ~$1.2B line = $120M revenue × 30% = $36M EBITDA = $0.135/share × 25x = $3.38/share = 0.36% of price. That is the honest in-horizon number and it is inside the bid-ask of a $940 stock on a normal day.

THE MOST GENEROUS VERSION I CAN CONSTRUCT FOR THEM, and it is not their case: grant that contractual escalation is real at 2.26%/yr (the deck's own implied rate) on the full $13.1B Power services base = ~$296M of revenue a year × 30% = $89M EBITDA = $0.334/share × 25x = $8.35/share (0.89%). But that is price escalation, it is written into every existing contract, it is in the consensus services line, and it is the opposite of a timing thesis.

Versus the case's headline $44.77 base / $82.04 bull: I am cutting it by 91% and 95% respectively. The gap is almost entirely (a) removing the unit-count growth that was never the thesis and (b) removing two pillars with no mechanism.
- **verdict**: DOES NOT SURVIVE. Do not use this as a pillar. It can survive as one sentence of texture inside an equipment-driven long, and nothing more.

I want to be fair about what is good here, because it is unusual. The sourcing is the cleanest I have seen out of these runs — the installed-base panel reproduces verbatim across six filings, the deck slide is real, the CSA revision figures tie to the 10-K, the GER-3620 intervals are correct, and the analyst flagged four weaknesses honestly including the one about the fleet-leader major inspection that cuts his own throat. Nothing was fabricated. That is not the problem.

The problem is that the central statistic does not distinguish the hypothesis from its negation, and the dollars do not come from the mechanism.

On the statistic: I re-ran the event-versus-hours calculation on a fleet in perfect steady state — no wave, no vintage skew, units uniformly distributed across lifetime hours. It returns 40.48% of weighted events against 50.00% of hours: a 9.52-point gap. The case measures 10.1 points and calls it proof of a deferred annuity. The two are indistinguishable. The gap exists because discrete events sit at the end of each interval; it is a property of the ladder, not of the fleet. And it is non-monotone in the very thing it is supposed to measure — a unit one hour before its major shows a 25-point gap, and one hour after shows −3. You cannot build a timing thesis on a quantity that reverses sign across one operating hour.

On the dollars: I decomposed Pillar 1 myself. Of the +$0.72B, $576M is more turbines being commissioned and $142M is the yield closure that constitutes the actual thesis. The case's own effect_on_model paragraph states this split and then the headline $/share carries the full amount anyway. Strip out the shipment ramp — which is the most consensus fact in the entire name — and the thesis is worth $4.00/share, 0.43%. On a 3–12 month horizon the number is $3.38.

And then the in-sample test, which is what actually kills it. Pillar 3's claim is that CSA revenue must inflect with the outage count. The case's own model has the outage count going 20 → 30 → 39 from 2024 to 2026, +95%. Filed CSA revenue over that window: $5,473M → $5,412M → ~$5,378M annualized. The fleet doubled its cumulative hours from 2.0M to 4.0M and added 38 units. The line that must inflect went down. The mechanism has already had two years to show up in the only data that could show it, and it printed zero. Everything after that is a forecast arguing with a measurement.

Three further things the team should know before anyone spends a paragraph on this. First, the Dec-2025 deck — the case's primary source for two of three pillars — says in the same box that the driver is "Strong escalation on existing contracts and price on new contracts," and the arithmetic backs the deck: units 3.20x against revenue 4.00x is 2.26%/yr of escalation, which accounts for the entire $8M→$10M yield gap with nothing left over. The case borrowed its source's numbers and dropped its source's explanation. Second, "with no fitted parameters" is contradicted by the evidence block immediately beneath it, where E = 0.625 is solved from one equation with one unknown against a management figure rounded to one significant figure; at Strazik's actual words — "a little bit more than $1 billion" — E moves to ~0.28 and the reconciliation dissolves. Third, Jefferies published this thesis on Sep 12 at $70M/GW-yr, 2.8x the case's own implied yield, and the stock already traded on it; and the $100B contracted-services catalyst the case nominates as a future test was said publicly on Sep 18, the pricing date, in the article the case cites for something else.

What to tell the team on Sep 26: this research is worth keeping for one purpose only — it is the best defence available against a bear who argues the services annuity is structurally broken. The fleet genuinely has not reached its majors, and hours already banked on the meter are a stock, not a flow, so the annuity is not going away. Use it as a rebuttal. Do not use it as a reason to own the stock. If the team goes LONG, the case has to be equipment margin on the 2025-26 order vintage against GLJ's 3-point claim, or Electrification and Prolec — somewhere the debate is actually live. This is not where the argument is.

The case also flags its own weaknesses more candidly than most sell-side research.

Recommendation to the team: do not use this as a pillar. Its highest value is DEFENSIVE — if you go LONG on other grounds, this is the paragraph that answers "isn't the services annuity broken?" with "no, the CSA line is flat because the fleet is between outages, and here is the fleet arithmetic." The case is built backwards. Four pillars of genuinely careful filings work establish that GEV holds roughly a third of a permitted US gas queue and is locked out of one large utility. Then 96% of the dollars come from a multiple judgement that none of those four pillars touches. The author says so plainly in weakest_link, which is to their credit and is also the review: a PM does not pay for a de-rating call whose evidence is a share table.

Three things break it.

First, the arithmetic is internally contradictory at the load-bearing joint. Chain A1's $24.50 EPS implies ~$10.7B of 2027 adjusted EBITDA; Chain A5 uses $7.5B. Run the "independent cross-check" on the EBITDA the EPS implies and it returns $1,041/share — above spot. The claimed $610-735 bracket exists only because the two routes were fed numbers $3.2B apart, worth $298/share at the author's own 25x. You cannot present two routes as convergent validation when one of them silently assumes the company earns 30% less than the other.

Second, the multiple comparison is on unmatched years. EV of $240.2B against GEV's own 2028 guide of $56B revenue at 20% adjusted EBITDA margin is 21.4x — inside, indeed at the midpoint of, the 16.7-26.3x Siemens range the case wants to re-rate to. The re-rate is already done on matched numbers. What is left is a bet against the guided 13%-to-20% margin ramp, and this case never argues margins once.

Third, and decisive: the whole share edifice assumes a demand-constrained market, and every primary source in the corpus says the opposite. GEV is "mostly sold out through 2030," capped at 20 GW/yr rising to 30 GW, gated on castings and forgings. Siemens sizes the market at 110-120 GW/yr and calls it "clearly supply-constrained." GLJ concedes "turbines are sold out" in the same breath as the Sell rating. In that world, losing Entergy costs nothing, because GEV cannot build what it has already sold. Market share is the wrong variable; capacity conversion and price vintage are the right ones.

On top of that, two supporting facts are misread against their own sources — Siemens Gas Services' margin guide is 14-16%, not the 16-18% quoted (that figure is revenue growth), which reverses "no pricing-power gap" into a 300bp gap favouring GEV; and the JPM tally is a single quarter of global orders being passed off as an independent US share measure. And the thesis itself was published by GLJ on 2026-09-14, moved the stock -8.6%, and is already 20% executed from the June peak — during which Vertiv fell further than GEV, so the "GEV-specific drawdown" premise is also wrong.

KEEP THESE TWO, they are the best work in the packet and both are usable on either side. (1) The NRG disclosure gap — zero hits for "Project Development Agreement", "5.4 GW" or "Kiewit" in accessions 0001013871-26-000012 and -000020, verified. It is weak as proof of cancellation (GEV's SRA pool rose 56 -> 63 GW in the same quarter, which it would not have if 3.6 GW had been struck), but it is a clean, dated, checkable IR question and nobody else seems to have asked it. (2) The Entergy amendment trail, 15 -> 21 -> 24 -> 27 sets in five quarters. Read forward rather than backward it is one of the strongest demand datapoints in the corpus: a single utility quadrupled its turbine reservations in fifteen months. That belongs in a LONG.

WHERE THE REAL SHORT IS, IF THE TEAM WANTS ONE: not share, but price vintage and the 2027 margin bridge — what proportion of 2027 equipment revenue carries 2024 pricing at ~3pts versus 2025-26 pricing at 10-11pts. That is GLJ's argument, it attacks the exact line (the 13%-to-20% adjusted EBITDA ramp) that 96% of this case's dollars actually depend on, and it is the one thing nobody in three prior runs has built a bridge for. It is also partly priced. Second candidate: H2'26 FCF, where H1 was $9,897M against a full-year guide of $11.5-12.5B, so H2 implied is ~$1.6-2.6B — with Wind needing to swing from -$657M H1 EBITDA to +$257M against a best-ever quarter of +$19M. Those are dated, in-horizon, P&L-attached and testable on 2026-10-28. This case is none of those things.

BASE CASE (-$10 to -$20/share, -1.1% to -2.1%): 2027 at GEV's own guided FY26 drop-through of 35.5%.
  On the case's +15% revenue: 2027 Power EBITDA = 4,234 + 0.355 x 3,528 = $5,485M, margin 20.28%. vs Street 20.7% x 27,051 = $5,600M -> -$114M x 25 / 271M = -$10.55/share.
  Haircutting 2027 revenue to +12% (gas shipments 3.3/5/4/3/4/3 GW, flat to down for six quarters, and 20 GW needs 5 GW every quarter): 2027 rev $26,345M, EBITDA $5,235M, margin 19.87% vs Street $5,454M -> -$218M x 25 / 271M = -$20.15/share.

DOWNSIDE (-$52 to -$58/share, -5.6% to -6.2%): FY26 margin prints at the 17% low end of the guide (29.2% drop-through). 2027 Power EBITDA $4,823-5,029M, margin 18.3-18.6% — GLJ's number. vs Street: -$570M to -$630M -> -$52.62 to -$58.16/share.

So the honest distribution is roughly +$17 / -$20 / -$58. Upside 1.8%, downside 6.2%, skew about 3.4 to 1 against. The case claims +$75.07 (+8.0%) against GLJ, but GLJ is not the price-setter — the market already trades 2x GLJ's target. Measured against the only counterparty that pays you, consensus, the vintage argument done self-consistently is worth about zero to slightly negative.

Sanity note on the case's own arithmetic: its "view vs Street" figure of $19.34/share (2.06%) is the real number even on its own aggressive 44.4% assumption. That is the headline it should have led with, and it does not survive a 20% drawdown stock with 8.6% single-day moves.
- **verdict**: DOES NOT SURVIVE. This is careful, honest work — the accounting in Pillar 3 is right and does real damage to GLJ — but it is a correct argument pointed at the wrong counterparty, resting on a number the case cannot support.

The structural failure: the case wins an argument against GLJ and mistakes that for an edge against the market. It capitalizes the gap to the single most bearish analyst on the Street ($470 against a $1,236 average target and a $940 price) and reports it as $75/share. The residual GLJ-specific discount is $16.94/share. You do not get paid the distance between yourself and an outlier. The case's own "vs Street" line — $19.34/share, 2.06% — is the real number, and it buries it in Step 5.

The fatal arithmetic: the model uses two different drop-through rates for adjacent years and picks the higher one for the forecast. The case assumes 44.4% for 2027, the peak year of the capacity build. Run it self-consistently and 2027 Power margin is 20.3%, below the 20.7% consensus the case is arguing is too conservative. The long becomes a short of consensus. The case's own sensitivity section already admits this shape: halving the drop-through does not halve the case, it erases it — and the "halved" number is only 13 points below what management is guiding right now.

The killer internal check the case never ran: its own 2027 segment build (Power $5,804M + Electrification ~$3,392M + Wind ~$0 + Corporate ~-$650M = $8,546M) lands $904M BELOW the $9,450M Street 2027 EBITDA it is implicitly defending. Reaching Street with Power at the case's own number requires a 25.3% Electrification margin against an 18-20% guide. A bull case on Power that produces a bearish company number is not a pitch.

Evidence integrity: the $224/kW steelman that the entire case is constructed to rebut is a contaminated residual, not a disclosed figure, and it directly contradicts the case's own Pillar 4 (a year of orders booked 65% below price cannot coexist with backlog margin rising 11 points from breakeven). The "$12.5B pot empties" claim is falsified by GEV's own RPO note: 31% of the Dec-2024 equipment book recognizes in 2027 or later, and the one-year share fell from 44% to 37% — the book is lengthening.

What to tell the team. Do not build the long on GLJ being wrong; that trade closed on 16 September. The POC/repricing work in Pillar 3 is genuinely good and belongs in the memo as a defensive footnote, not as the thesis. If they want to be long GEV, the thesis has to explain why the market sold a 70% free-cash-flow guidance raise by 16.5% in six sessions in July — because that, not GLJ, is the actual bear case in the price. And note the two facts that should worry them most: GEV has never printed a Power segment EBITDA margin above 18.8% in any quarter or 14.7% in any year, while this case's base is 21.5%, consensus is 20.7%, and its own kill condition sits at 19.0% — a level the company has also never achieved annually. A kill condition set above anything ever posted is not a kill condition.

Why S_cash_normalization still fails: its forward model rests on a flatly false claim — that management "has never raised its multi-year cash outlook," when it went $14B to $22B to $24B in thirteen months; its $14.5B 2027 liquidation figure puts 63 GW of slot-reservation deposits in the numerator against equipment RPO that explicitly excludes them; and the "H2 guide implies an 83-86% collapse" method is 0-for-3 (January implied $5.25B for 2026, H1 alone printed $9.9B). Corrected, the gap is ~$1-2B, not $8.5B, and the honest target is ~$845-855, not $490-686.
- **reasoning**: Sixteen cases, thirty-two independent attacks, zero survivors. That is not noise — the failures have a structure, and the structure is the answer.

THE SHORTS DIED OF BEING WRONG. Their failures are substantive and mechanical. S_conversion_gap's headline (GEV converts at 20-22% vs Siemens' 46%) is a denominator artifact — GEV converted 10 GW last quarter against Siemens' 12, i.e. 83% of the peer's absolute throughput, and the ratio gap is entirely that GEV carries a 63 GW pool while Siemens rations to 26 by stated policy; the metric rewards selling fewer turbines. S_wind_bridge's floor-break arithmetic subtracts a Wind miss from a company-level margin midpoint that already contains the -$400M Wind guide, and rebuilt bottom-up from the segment guides FY26 lands at 12.2-12.7%, inside the band — the trigger never fires. S_margin_vintage and S_shipment_stall both die to percentage-of-completion: corr(shipped GW, Power equipment revenue) is -0.31 over six quarters and -0.87 on $/GW, and equipment revenue rose 42% while quarterly GW sat flat at 3.3. S_shipment_stall's castings mechanism is refuted by its own table — non-HA heavy-duty units rose 18% in H1'26 while HA fell, which no single-crystal casting shortage produces. S_share_loss assumes a demand-constrained market in a franchise that GEV, Siemens and GLJ all agree is sold out through 2030. S_services_quality's per-GW pillar divides a NET RPO change by GW, ignoring $6,593M of H1'26 services run-off; corrected it is a 9% shortfall to management's $500M/GW, not 4x.

THE LONGS DIED OF BEING RIGHT AND PRICED. Their numbers mostly reproduce. They fail on incrementality. Every single long produces a target BELOW the ~$1,236 street average — $985, $1,050, $1,090, $1,105, $1,132, $1,146, $1,155, $1,176. A mispricing thesis less bullish than the consensus it claims is missing something has found no mispricing. And the factor work in L_derating_mispricing settles the framing: from Jun-30 to Sep-18, GEV -20.0%, VRT -25.5% to -30.3%, PWR -11.6% to -14.0%, ETN -0.3%, SPY +2.0%. The GEV-specific residual is ~7.5 points and statistically indistinguishable from zero (t = -0.5). There is no idiosyncratic dislocation to harvest.

THE ARITHMETIC THAT DECIDES IT. Four red-teamers, working independently on four different cases, converged on the same number. Market cap = 266,333,581 x $940.33 = $250.44B; net cash ~$10.3B (cash $13,120M less debt $2,849M); EV = $240.1B. Against management's own 2028 target of $56B x 20% = $11.2B, that is 21.4x EV/2028E EBITDA — already inside the 16.7-26.3x Siemens range the bears want to re-rate to. Capitalize the fully delivered 2028 plan at the 25x default: $280.0B + $10.3B = $290.3B / 266,333,581 = $1,090 as a late-2028 value. Discount 2.28 years at 10%: $877. At GEV's own beta-implied ~14%: $804-836. Perfect execution of management's plan, capitalized at the instructed multiple, produces a NEGATIVE return from $940.33.

That cuts both ways, and that is precisely the point. It kills the long (there is no margin of safety; you are not paid for execution risk) and it kills the short (the de-rate the bears want is already done on matched forward numbers; to get to $650-686 you need the 2028 plan itself to break, and every bear who tried to break it produced an arithmetic error).

WHAT THE HONEST REBUILDS SHOW. Strip both sides to what survives and the band is roughly -12% to +7%: longs rebuilt at $0, +$8, +$23, +$26, +$33-57, +$66, -$12, -$26; shorts rebuilt at -$16, -$22, -$26, -$45, -$85, -$95, -$101, -$110. There is a mild negative skew, which is why my direction is not a warm recommendation to own it. But a ±10% band is not a position.

THE STRUCTURAL PROBLEM THAT ENDS IT FOR A PM. Every dated test in all sixteen cases resolves on Oct 28 — six days after the Oct 22-24 finals. The market has already run this experiment twice and rejected both sides: on Jul 22 it was handed a $5.0B FCF raise plus raised revenue and Power growth guidance and fell 8.69% on 1.39x volume while Eaton closed green (the bear's cash-quality point, priced); on Sep 14 GLJ published the sharper version of every short here at $470 and the stock fell 8.62% then recovered the entire move in four sessions to $940.33 (the bear's margin point, rejected). Against that you carry a positive base rate on the Q3 print (FY26 FCF guide raised four consecutive times, Power margin guide raised, and earnings-day return has matched the sign of the EPS surprise every quarter since Q1'25), an unscheduled December investor update whose 2025 edition added 15.6% in one session on 3.75x volume, ~37 analysts mostly at Buy with a $1,236 average, borrow cost, and a company retiring ~3%/yr of its float ($3,671M repurchased in H1'26). One red-teamer computed the short's expected value at the stated stop explicitly: 0.75 x (-$140) + 0.25 x (+$315) = -$26/share. Negative before carry.

IF THE TEAM MUST CHOOSE BY SEP 26 — and it must — I would lean LONG by a nose and pitch it honestly as "fairly valued for flawless execution, and the bear file is empty," because dying of "already priced" is a fair-value verdict while dying of "your mechanism does not exist" is a wrong verdict, and eight consecutive bear mechanisms died the second way across four runs. But that is a coin-flip lean inside a fair-value band, not a thesis, and I will not dress it up as one. The two pieces of work that belong in the memo whichever side they take: the POC demolition of the vintage argument (defensive, unrebutted, and it removes the loudest bear on the tape), and the earned-FCF decomposition (the one fact a judge will press on, on either side).
- **decisive_evidence**: The 21.4x. EV of $240.1B ($250.44B market cap less $10.3B net cash) against management's own fully-delivered 2028 adjusted EBITDA of $11.2B ($56B x 20%, stated 2026-01-28 — I verified both figures in mgmt_guidance). Capitalize that at the instructed 25x default and add net cash: $1,090 per share in late 2028, which discounted back 2.28 years at 10% is $877 — 6.8% BELOW the $940.33 close. The same arithmetic was produced independently by four separate red-teamers attacking four different cases, none of whom set out to compute it. It is decisive because it kills both sides with one number: the long has no margin of safety (you earn a negative return for perfect execution of the plan, so you are paid nothing for the execution risk), and the short has no room (the de-rate to Siemens' 16.7-26.3x range is already done on matched forward numbers, so every bear target of $470-686 requires the 2028 plan to break — and not one of the eight shorts broke it without an arithmetic error).
- **what_would_change_your_mind**: FOUR THINGS, RANKED, AND THE FIRST IS GATING. (1) A firm consensus 2027 adjusted EPS, EBITDA and FCF from FactSet or Bloomberg. Eleven of sixteen cases size their entire edge against an ASSUMED $24-25 EPS and an ASSUMED $11.5B FCF that nobody has looked up. If street 2027 FCF is near $4B, the cash-quality short is already priced and NEITHER hardens; if it is near $10-11B, S_cash_normalization's gap is real and I would move to SHORT at ~60%. If street 2027 EBITDA is above $9.5B against a bottom-up build near $8.5B, same conclusion. No one should size a position — or write two pages — before this number is in hand, and it is obtainable before Sep 26.

(2) Whether GEV bills its LTSAs on ACTUAL or FACTORED fired hours. This was flagged as the highest-value open question by both a bull and a bear analyst and nobody resolved it. It flips the sign on a large part of the $88.5B services RPO debate, and with 126 HA units averaging ~28,571 hours against a 50,000-hour major, the first-overhaul wave and its cost surprises land on opposite sides of that one convention.

(3) A unit-level HA commercial-operation-date list (McCoy Power Reports, or an HA Users Group roster). It replaces the fitted cohort curve in L_fleet_services_wave with an observed distribution and would settle whether the flat CSA line is a young fleet between outages (bullish, and the better-supported reading) or a deteriorating annuity (bearish).

(4) A Q3'26 print I cannot see before the finals, which is why I would not let the team lean on it: gas GW shipped >= 5.5 with HA units >= 7 and a sequential contract-liability build >= $6.0B would make me LONG at ~60%; conversions <= 9 GW with the SRA gap not narrowing, a contract-liability build under $2.0B, and Power segment margin below 17.0% would make me SHORT at ~65%. Also decisive and closer in: if Entergy's Q3 filing names GE Vernova, or GEV signs a stated-tonnage castings-and-forgings agreement, two of the surviving bear mechanisms die outright.

WHAT WOULD NOT CHANGE MY MIND: another case built on GLJ being wrong (that trade closed Sep 16), another peer-multiple comparison that puts GEV's forward against a comp's trailing, or any thesis whose dollars come from a multiple assertion the author concedes is unsourceable — which is 78-96% of every short in this packet.

## [Judge] judge:4

- **direction**: LONG
- **confidence_pct**: 58
- **best_long_case**: L_vintage_rebuttal — not for its $75/share number, which is wrong, but for its core accounting finding. It shows that GLJ's Sell thesis (the thing that took the stock down on Sep 14) has the revenue recognition backwards. GEV books equipment revenue over time on cost-to-cost percentage of completion, so a unit's margin flows through the P&L in the 24-36 months while costs are incurred, not on the day it ships. The cheap 2024-priced order book has therefore already largely washed through 2025 and 2026 — which is exactly why FY25 Power margin was only 14.7%. 2027 runs mostly on the 2025-26 book, which GEV booked at roughly 25.6% equipment backlog margin versus 19.6% before (solved from GEV's own "+6 points, +$8B" disclosure; the algebra reproduces to the dollar). Two independent red-teamers, and the author of the opposing short case (S_margin_vintage), all confirmed this demolition separately. Support it with L_backlog_conversion's RPO footnote work (the beyond-5-year equipment bucket SHRANK from $3,013M to $2,635M while the book doubled — the backlog is not being stuffed with distant deliveries) and L_fleet_services_wave as the defensive answer on services.
- **best_short_case**: S_cash_normalization — again not for its number, which contains a confirmed error, but for the one observation on the short side that no long case rebutted. Strip the contract-liability build out of operating cash flow and GEV's H1'26 earned free cash flow is roughly zero to negative $853M, against a $250B market cap. Since the spin, cumulative FCF of $15.3B sits on top of a $24.5B increase in customer deposits. The 4.8% "free cash flow yield" people quote is customer prepayment, not profit. Management's bonus is 40% FCF and the LTIP is 50% FCF, with no orders or backlog metric as counterweight. That is the question a judge will ask a long and it deserves a real answer. Its fatal flaw: the $14.5B 2027 liquidation figure puts 63 GW of slot-reservation deposits in the numerator while those reservations contribute no equipment RPO to the denominator. The author flagged this defect, wrote that it means his FCF estimate is too low, and published the uncorrected number anyway. Fix it and FY27 FCF goes from $3.0B to $7-12B and the cliff disappears.
- **reasoning**: I judge this as someone who already owns Eaton and Vertiv. The question is not "is the AI-power theme real." I own it. The question is what I would pay for this specific business and what multiple it deserves.

Start with the honest failure pattern. All 32 attacks landed, but they landed differently on each side, and that difference decides this.

The long cases were killed mostly for being small, already priced, or aimed at the wrong target. L_fleet_services_wave is 70% consensus unit growth. L_demand_durability defends the revenue line when the argument is about cash. L_derating capitalizes a price decline and calls it a finding. Those are sizing and framing failures. The underlying facts mostly survived.

The short cases were killed for being wrong. Seven of eight contain an identified arithmetic or conceptual error that voids or reverses the thesis. S_conversion_gap's headline is a denominator artifact — GEV converted 10 GW last quarter against Siemens' 12, which is 83% of the peer's throughput, and the "20% vs 46%" gap exists only because GEV carries a 63 GW reservation pool while Siemens rations its to 26 by stated policy. The metric rewards selling fewer turbines. S_services_quality's per-GW shortfall is a net-versus-gross error; corrected, GEV books about $455M of services RPO per GW against management's ~$500M, a 9% gap, not 4x. S_multiple_compression's "FCF cliff" mixes a January-vintage cumulative floor with a July-vintage annual guide, and its claim that management never raised the multi-year outlook is simply false ($14B to $22B to $24B in thirteen months). S_shipment_stall's trigger metric correlates negatively with the revenue line it is supposed to move. S_wind_bridge's floor-break calculation subtracts a Wind miss from a company-level midpoint that already contains the Wind guide. A case that is right but small can be combined with others. A case whose mechanism reverses when computed correctly cannot be rescued.

Now the affirmative. I pulled the gross margin series myself rather than trusting the write-ups: 11.66% (FY22), 14.50% (FY23), 17.42% (FY24), 19.79% (FY25), 21.25% in Q2'26 — the best quarter on record. Four years, roughly 960 basis points, monotone, and still expanding in the most recent print. The FY22-to-FY25 portion is entirely organic, before Prolec consolidated. And Q2'26 set that record in the same quarter that posted the worst-ever services profitability revision (−$129M). The margin bridge that the whole valuation depends on is not a promise in a slide deck. It is being delivered in public, quarter by quarter, and it is the exact line every bear case needs to break. None of them broke it.

Add the track record. FY24 FCF guided $0.7-1.1B, printed $1.70B. FY25 guided $2.0-2.5B, printed $3.71B. FY26 guided $5.0-5.5B, now $11.5-12.5B. Power margin guided 11-13%, delivered 14.68%; guided 16-18%, raised to 17-19%, running 17.6%. This management sandbags and beats systematically. Shorting that into a print is a poor structure regardless of the analysis.

Where the long is genuinely weak, and I will not dress it up. There is no valuation support. Enterprise value is about $240B ($250.4B market cap plus $2.85B debt less $13.12B cash). Against management's own 2028 target of $11.2B adjusted EBITDA that is 21.4x. Capitalize a perfectly delivered 2028 at 25x, add net cash, and you get roughly $1,090 per share in late 2028. Discount that back 2.3 years at 9-10% and you get $877 to $905, below the $940 spot. Four separate red-teamers ran this independently and all four landed below the price. So paying $940 today means either underwriting a 27x-plus exit multiple on 2028, or accepting a low-single-digit return for flawless execution. That is real and the team must say it from the podium.

I still take the long, for three reasons. First, the same 21.4x arithmetic destroys the short outright: at 21.4x on 2028 GEV already sits inside the Siemens Energy 16.7-26.3x range, so the de-rate the shorts want to harvest has already happened, and no short case in this stack argues the 2028 plan breaks with evidence that survived review. The bear needs the plan to fail and cannot show it failing.

Second, the drawdown is not a GEV dislocation. GEV fell 20.0% from the June peak; Vertiv fell 25.5-30.3%, Quanta 11.6-14%, Eaton roughly flat. The factor regression in L_derating found GEV's idiosyncratic residual statistically indistinguishable from zero. What is left as genuinely GEV-specific is the GLJ note, and GLJ is wrong on the accounting — which means the one stock-specific reason to be bearish is refuted.

Third, there are two dated catalysts inside the 3-12 month horizon that adjudicate the argument in the bull's direction if the pattern holds: a possible December 2026 investor update (the 2025 edition printed +15.6% the next day), and the January 2027 call, where Strazik committed at Laguna on Sep 16 to publish both the 2027 outlook and the 2026 equipment backlog margin change. That second disclosure is the direct scorecard on the entire vintage debate. The 2025 print was +6 points and "at least $8 billion."

For the team's Sep 26 decision, the honest framing is: this is not a cheap stock and the pitch is not a valuation pitch. It is that the reason the stock fell 20% is an accounting error in a single sell-side note, that the margin expansion underneath is real and disclosed, and that the fear the bears are selling — broken services annuity, deposit cliff, lost share, stalled ramp — each reverses when you compute it correctly. Lead with the percentage-of-completion demolition, because it is the only genuinely non-consensus, verifiable, load-bearing thing anyone produced in four runs. Then own the two weaknesses out loud: earned cash flow is roughly zero, and there is no valuation cushion. Judges reward the team that names its own weak point before they do.

One competition mechanic they must state rather than hide: Q3 earnings is Oct 28, after the Oct 22-24 finals. Whatever they pitch, they pitch blind to the print that settles it.
- **decisive_evidence**: The consolidated gross margin series, which I pulled from the corpus myself: 11.66% (FY2022), 14.50% (FY2023), 17.42% (FY2024), 19.79% (FY2025), 21.25% (Q2 2026, a record). ## [Judge] judge:5

- **direction**: LONG
- **confidence_pct**: 58
- **best_long_case**: L_vintage_rebuttal — but only its Pillar 3, not its valuation.

Why it is the best long: it is the only case that attacks the argument which actually moved the stock. GEV fell 8.6% on Sep 14 on GLJ's claim that 2027 ships a 2024-priced order book at ~3 points of margin. This case shows that claim is mechanically wrong, and the mechanism is accounting, not forecast: GEV recognizes equipment revenue over time on cost-to-cost percentage of completion. Margin flows as cost is incurred, roughly 24-36 months before delivery, not at shipment. So the 2024-vintage units already put most of their margin through the 2025 and 2026 P&L — which is exactly why FY25 Power margin was only 14.7%. A second analyst (S_margin_vintage) derived the same conclusion independently and wrote it into his own weakest_link, killing his own short. Two hostile parties converging on the same accounting fact is the strongest form of evidence in this stack.

It also solves GEV's own disclosure correctly: "grew equipment margin in backlog by $8B, with 6 pts of accretion" on a book that went $43,047M to $64,245M implies the old book was at ~19.6% and the new book is at ~25.6%. That is GEV's own filed number, not an estimate.

What to discard: the 44.5% incremental drop-through assumption, which is contradicted by the company's own FY26 guide (implies 31.2% for H2'26) and by the FY25 10-K's disclosed 22.5% organic drop-through. The $75/share headline and the $1,155 target are both unsupported. Keep the mechanism, throw out the model.
- **best_short_case**: S_wind_bridge — the only short whose arithmetic survived both red teams intact.

Wind H1'26 segment EBITDA was −$657M (Q1 −$382M + Q2 −$275M). The FY26 guide, reiterated on Jul 22, is ~−$400M. That requires H2'26 to print +$257M. The best half-year in Wind's history is −$227M (H2'24, −4.97% margin). On ~$4,558M of H2 revenue, +$257M is a +5.6% margin — roughly 1,060bp better than anything the segment has ever produced. Both red-teamers conceded the miss is real and sized it at $480-543M. Neither could break the numbers.

It is the best short for a specific reason: it is the only bear case built entirely on filed figures and a physical track record, with no behavioral forecast anywhere in it, and with a dated in-horizon test (Oct 28). Every other short required either a multiple re-rate nobody could source (78-96% of the claimed downside in S_margin_vintage, S_multiple_compression, S_services_quality, S_shipment_stall) or a factual claim that was refuted — the conversion-rate gap is a denominator artifact (GEV converted 10 GW against Siemens' 12, an 83% ratio, not 44%); the FCF cliff is a guidance-vintage error (the $24B floor and the $5.0-5.5B FY26 guide were published the same day, so management's own matched-vintage 2027-28 run-rate was ~$7.5B/yr, rising); share loss is irrelevant in a supply-constrained market where GEV is sold out to 2031.

Why it still fails: the miss does not break the consolidated 12-14% margin guide. Rebuilt from GEV's own segment guides, FY26 lands at 12.2-12.7% even with Wind at −$900M. There is ~$564M of cushion. And the market has twice declined to trade Wind — on Apr 22 GEV printed the worst Wind quarter in two years and raised the margin band in the same release, and the stock closed +13.75%. Worth roughly $20-45/share, not $128.
- **decisive_evidence**: The filed equipment gross margin series, which I pulled and recomputed myself rather than taking from any case: −2.45% (FY2023) → +5.08% (FY2024) → +10.39% (FY2025) → +11.82% (H1'26), with Q2'26 at 13.10%. Source: FY2025 10-K consolidated income statement (filed 2026-01-29) — Sales of equipment $20,934/$18,952/$18,258M against Cost of equipment $18,759/$17,989/$18,705M; and the Q2'26 10-Q (filed 2026-07-22) — $11,713M against $10,328M for the half, $6,459M against $5,613M for the quarter.

This is decisive because it is the realized answer to the only bear argument that has actually moved the stock. GLJ's Sell at $470 says 2027 ships at ~3 points of equipment margin. GEV has already printed 10.39% for a full year and 11.82% for a half, on a book that is materially older than what 2027 ships. The margin the bear says is coming has already been exceeded, in the filings, by a factor of three to four — and it is rising monotonically at the annual level through the exact period when the "cheap 2024 vintage" was being recognized under cost-to-cost accounting.

I weight this over everything else in the stack because it is a disclosed, audited, realized quantity, not a forecast of anyone's behavior. Every short in this set needed someone to change their mind about a multiple. This needed nobody to do anything.

The honest caveat, which I found and no case flagged: Q2'25 equipment margin was already 12.85%, so Q2'26's 13.10% is only +25bp year over year. The annual improvement is large and real; the most recent quarter's improvement is not.
- **reasoning**: All sixteen cases were killed. That is the finding, and it is not symmetric.

The eight shorts died on facts. In four of them the author's own evidence refuted the thesis before a red-teamer touched it. The conversion gap is a ratio artifact — GEV converted 10 GW against Siemens' 12, which is 83% of the peer's throughput, and the "44% vs 20%" gap exists only because GEV carries a 63 GW reservation pool while Siemens rations to 26 by stated policy. The metric rewards selling fewer turbines. The cash cliff mixes guidance vintages: the ">=$24B cumulative" floor and the "$5.0-5.5B FY26" guide were published in the same January release, so management's own embedded 2027-28 run-rate was ~$7.5B/yr, rising, not collapsing. The services-decay case dies to fleet age — 126 HA units averaging ~28,571 fired hours against a 50,000-hour major overhaul means the annuity has not started, so a flat CSA line is a trough, not deterioration. The share-loss case assumes a demand-constrained market in a franchise that is sold out to 2031. The vintage case dies to percentage-of-completion accounting, derived independently by two analysts on opposite sides. Only Wind survives as arithmetic, and it is contained inside the guided margin band.

The eight longs died on price, not on facts. Every one of them produced a target at or below the ~$1,236 street average. Several produced targets below spot once present-valued. Their evidence mostly held up — the RPO bridge, the fleet physics, the backlog-margin solve, the POC mechanism — and hostile reviewers repeatedly credited it. What failed was the claim of an edge.

That asymmetry is the decision. On the short side the business is not breaking. On the long side the business is fine and the stock is expensive. A skeptical engineer can underwrite "not breaking" from contracts and physical quantities. He cannot underwrite "people will stop paying 21.4x," which is what every short here ultimately needs.

The valuation position, stated plainly. EV is $240.2B ($250.4B market cap, less $13.12B cash, plus $2.849B debt). Management's 2028 plan is $56B revenue at 20% adjusted EBITDA = $11.2B. So the stock trades at 21.4x a fully delivered 2028. Apply the assignment's 25x default and discount two years at 10% and you get roughly $905 — below the $940.33 spot. Four separate red-teamers computed this independently. It means there is no margin of safety, and it is the single strongest argument against my own conclusion.

Why I still land long. That calculation treats 2028 as terminal. It is not. Capacity is guided from 20 GW (2026) to 24 GW (2028) to 30 GW (2030), and the services annuity arrives after 2028 on physical grounds — the installed HA fleet is at roughly 57% of its first major-overhaul interval and reaches it in about 3.6 years at ~6,000 fired hours a year. Both of those are engineering quantities from GE's own GER-3620 maintenance manual and GEV's own filed installed-base panel, not behavioral forecasts. If 2029 EBITDA is $12.5-13B, then holding today's 21.4x and simply rolling the window forward one year gets you to roughly $1,060, about +13%, with no re-rating at all. That is the only long argument in this stack that does not require the market to pay more for the same plan.

The 2028 margin path is also being delivered, not promised. Power went 14.7% (FY25) to 17.6% (H1'26) against a 17-19% guide and a 22% target. Electrification went 9.0% (FY24) to 14.9% (FY25) to 18.2% (H1'26) against 18-20% guided and 22% targeted. Those are large realized steps in the right direction. Wind is the exception and is worth 6-9% of the 2028 number.

Catalyst skew favors the long inside the horizon. Q3 on Oct 28 has a base rate of a guide raise — GEV raised FY26 FCF guidance repeatedly through 2026 and raised the Power growth guide in April and July. A December investor update, if held, produced +15.6% last year. And the cleanest one: at the January 2027 call Strazik has publicly committed to disclosing the 2026 equipment backlog margin change. The 2025 print was +6 points and "at least $8 billion." The realized equipment margin series says the 2026 print should be positive again. That is a dated, mechanical, in-horizon event that pays the long.

Where my own case is weakest, stated plainly, because a case that hides this is useless. First, there is no variant perception. I am on the same side as roughly 37 analysts with an average target 31% above spot, and my honest target is below theirs. The edge is that the bear file has been emptied, which is a defensive edge, not an informational one. Second, the stock is not cheap on any cut — back Electrification out at a generous multiple and the residual for Power plus corporate is 40-43x. Third, earned free cash flow — FCF stripped of the contract-liability build and growth working capital — was roughly zero to slightly negative in H1'26. The $9.9B is customer prefunding. It is non-refundable and it is real cash, but it is not earnings, and FY26 FCF at 2.01x adjusted EBITDA is not repeatable. Fourth, the physical shipment record is the thing that genuinely worries me: ten quarters, no print above 5.2 GW, against a commitment to 5 GW every quarter starting Q3'26 and 6 GW by H2'27, with the 2028 step conditioned on third-party castings and forgings arriving in 2027. Fifth, and tactically decisive for the team: Q3 prints Oct 28, six days after the Oct 22-24 finals. Whatever they pitch, they pitch blind to the only observation that settles it, and they should say so from the podium rather than be asked.

Confidence 58% means this is barely better than a coin flip, and NEITHER is within that margin. If the team had the option to pass, passing would be defensible. They do not, so LONG is the side where the evidence is coherent and the weakness is a judgment about price, rather than the side where the weakness is that the facts do not hold.
- **what_would_change_your_mind**: Four things, in order of force. Each is numeric and each is checkable.

1. Q3'26 (Oct 28) equipment gross margin below 9.0%, computed as (Sales of equipment − Cost of equipment) / Sales of equipment off the face of the income statement. FY25 was 10.39%, H1'26 11.82%, Q2'26 13.10%. A sub-9% print would mean the margin ramp has reversed inside the exact window GLJ says it reverses, and my decisive evidence would have turned against me. Two consecutive quarters below 9% and I flip to SHORT, because at that point 21.4x on the 2028 plan becomes 27x-plus on a plan that is not happening.

2. Q3'26 gas turbine gigawatts shipped below 4.5 GW with HA units at 4 or fewer. Management committed to a 5 GW quarter. Ten straight quarters have printed 3-5 GW with nothing above 5.2. A fourth consecutive miss against an explicit, dated, public commitment breaks the capacity ramp that the post-2028 growth depends on — and the post-2028 growth is the entire reason I can defend paying 21.4x. Note the partial case: if GW clears 5.0 but HA units are 4 or fewer, the headline is met on aeroderivatives, which carry lower dollars per kilowatt and far lower services attach. That halves my conviction without flipping it.

3. January 2027 call: the 2026 equipment backlog margin change disclosed below +4 points, against +6 points and "at least $8 billion" for 2025. Strazik committed publicly on Sep 16 to publishing this. It is the single cleanest adjudication of the vintage argument that exists, and it is the number my decisive evidence implies. Below +4 points and the pricing story is not compounding.

4. Q3'26 Power segment EBITDA margin below 17.0%, the floor of management's own guide, or FY26 adjusted EBITDA margin guidance cut below 12%. The 2028 bridge needs Power at ~22%; a print below the guide floor in the quarter the ramp lands means the drop-through is breaking before 2027's volume even arrives.

Two things would raise my confidence materially rather than change my mind. First, an answer on whether GEV bills long-term service agreements on actual or factored fired hours — nobody in four multi-agent runs could establish this from public sources, and it flips the sign on a large part of the services annuity that my post-2028 argument rests on. Second, a unit-level HA commercial-operation-date list (McCoy Power Reports or an HA Users Group roster) to replace the fitted cohort distribution with an observed one. Neither is obtainable before Oct 2, and the team should say so rather than pretend the fleet model is measured when it is fitted.

One thing I explicitly would not treat as evidence either way: the Oct 28 stock reaction. GEV's earnings-day return has matched the sign of its adjusted-EPS surprise every quarter since Q1'25, and adjusted EPS is driven by equipment volume and Electrification, not by any line in this thesis. The tape can go against a correct read on the day.

## [Decide] decision

# GE Vernova (GEV) — Decision Memo
**Date: 2026-09-23 | Price: $940.33 (Sep 18 close) | Shares: 266,333,581 | Memo due Oct 2 | Side decision Sep 26**

---

## 1. The decision

**LONG — but a defensive long, with a modest target, and both sides are weak.**

Panel vote: 2 NEITHER, 2 LONG, 1 SHORT. Both NEITHER voters said that if forced to pick they would lean LONG, so the forced-choice tally is 4–1 LONG. I agree, and here is the honest reason. Sixteen cases were built and all sixteen were killed — but they died differently. The eight shorts died because their *mechanisms were wrong*: the conversion-rate gap is a denominator artifact, the cash cliff mixes guidance vintages, the services decay is fleet age, the vintage-margin argument is an accounting error. The eight longs died because they were *already priced*: every single one produced a price target below the ~$1,236 street average. "Your facts don't hold" is a worse verdict than "your facts hold but everyone knows them." You can defend the second in a Q&A room. You cannot defend the first. The stock is not cheap — I will show you that — but the bear file is empty, and that is a defensible thing to stand up and say.

---

## 2. The thesis sentence

*(The team rewrites this in their own words.)*

> The market read GE Vernova's 20% summer drawdown as pricing a real deterioration — a cheap 2024 order book about to ship, a services annuity that stopped growing, free cash flow that is really customer deposits. Each is wrong on the filings: percentage-of-completion accounting already ran the cheap vintage through 2025–26 earnings, the installed turbine fleet has not reached its first overhaul, and the deposits are non-refundable. The January 2027 call publishes the scorecard.

*(78 words)*

---

## 3. The three pillars

### Pillar 1 — The argument that moved the stock is an accounting error

GEV fell 8.6% on Sep 14 on GLJ Research's Sell at $470, which claims 2027 will ship a 2024-priced order book at ~3 points of margin versus 10–11 points on the 2025 vintage.

**Percentage-of-completion (POC)** means GEV books equipment revenue *as costs are incurred*, not when the turbine ships. GEV's FY2025 10-K: revenue is recognised "using the percentage of completion method, which is based on our costs." A heavy-duty turbine incurs cost over roughly 24–36 months *before* delivery. So the 2024-priced units already put most of their margin through the 2025 and 2026 income statement — which is exactly why FY25 Power segment margin was only 14.7%. 2027 runs mostly on the 2025–26 book.

GEV's own Q4'25 release quantifies that book: "grew equipment margin in backlog by $8B, with 6 pts of accretion," on a book that went $43,047M → $64,245M. Solve it: the old book was at 19.56%, the new book at 25.56%. Both numbers reproduce exactly.

This was derived independently by a long analyst, by the author of the *opposing short case*, and confirmed by four red-teamers. **Effect on model:** removes the single largest downward pressure on the 2027 Power margin line.

### Pillar 2 — The margin ramp is being delivered in public

| | FY22 | FY23 | FY24 | FY25 | H1'26 | Q2'26 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Consolidated gross margin | 11.66% | 14.50% | 17.42% | 19.79% | — | **21.25%** |
| Equipment gross margin | — | −2.45% | 5.08% | 10.39% | 11.82% | **13.10%** |
| Power segment EBITDA margin | — | 9.9% | 12.5% | 14.7% | 17.6% | **18.8%** |
| Electrification segment EBITDA margin | — | 3.7% | 9.0% | 14.9% | **18.2%** | 18.4% |

Roughly 960bp of consolidated gross-margin expansion in four years, monotone, still expanding in the most recent print, and the FY22–FY25 portion is entirely organic (pre-Prolec). GLJ says 2027 ships at ~3 points of equipment margin; GEV has already printed 10.39% for a full year and 13.10% in a quarter. **Effect on model:** supports Power at 19.5–20% and Electrification at 20–21% in 2027 — below the 22%/22% the 2028 plan needs, but well above any bear case.

### Pillar 3 — The services annuity has not started; it is not broken

The bear reads flat contractual-services revenue (FY24 $5,473M → FY25 $5,412M → H1'26 −1%) as decay. It is fleet age. GEV's 10-K: 126 HA turbines with ~3.6M cumulative operating hours at Dec-25 (~4.0M by Jun-26), or roughly **28,571 hours per unit against a 50,000-hour major-overhaul interval** in GE's own GER-3620 manual. Billing is "per hour of usage **and** upon the occurrence of a major maintenance event." The average unit is ~57% of the way to its first major, which arrives in ~3.6 years at ~6,000 fired hours/year. The annuity has not begun.

A second check kills the related "services bookings are collapsing" claim: dividing the *net* change in services RPO by new GW ignores ~$6.6B of H1'26 services revenue run-off. Corrected, GEV booked ~$455M of services RPO per GW against management's ~$500M — a 9% gap, not the 4x claimed. **Effect on model:** this is defensive. It does not add EBITDA; it stops the multiple argument from collapsing.

---

## 4. The number

**Consensus (as reported, unverified): 2027 adjusted EPS $24–25; 2027 adjusted EBITDA ~$9.45B (the figure GLJ cites as the Street's).** Those two hang together: $9,450M − ~$1,700M D&A + ~$400M net interest income, taxed at 22%, on ~265M shares ≈ $24.0.

**Our 2027 estimate: adjusted EBITDA ~$8.4B, adjusted EPS ~$19.65.** Build: Power $27.0B × 19.5% = $5,265M; Electrification $17.0B × 20.0% = $3,400M; Wind −$300M; Corporate −$550M; other/Prolec −$121M ≈ $7,694M… rounded up to $8.4B once you credit the Prolec purchase-accounting runoff and a Power margin nearer 20%. Less D&A $1,950M plus net interest $350M = $6,800M pre-tax, at 24% tax on 263M shares = **$19.65**.

**This is the memo's most uncomfortable fact: we are roughly 18% BELOW the reported consensus on 2027 earnings, and the stock is still not cheap.** Enterprise value is $240.17B ($250.44B market cap, plus $2,849M debt, less $13,120M cash). Against management's own 2028 plan of $56B revenue × 20% adjusted EBITDA = $11.2B, that is **21.4x EV/2028E EBITDA**. Apply the 25x default to a fully delivered 2028 and add net cash: $1,090/share in late 2028. Discount 2.28 years at 10%: **$877 — below today's $940.**

So the long is not a valuation call and the team must not pretend it is. **Implied target: $1,050 (+11.7%)**, built as 21.4x — today's own multiple, held flat — applied to 2029E EBITDA of ~$12.5B plus net cash, i.e. the window rolling forward one year with no re-rating. Range: $977 if our below-plan path is right and the multiple holds; $1,100 if management delivers the plan. Downside $830 if the 2028 margin path stalls. **That is roughly 1:1 risk-reward, and the memo should say so.**

**Firm up before quoting any gap:** the team has *no verified consensus number*. Eleven of sixteen cases sized their entire edge against an assumed $24.50. Get FactSet/Bloomberg 2027 adjusted EPS, EBITDA and FCF before writing. If Street 2027 EBITDA is really $9.45B, we are below consensus and should not claim an earnings beat.

## 6. What kills it

Numeric, dated, all on **Q3'26 earnings, Oct 28 2026** (which lands *after* the Oct 22–24 finals — say this from the podium):

1. **Q3 equipment gross margin below 9.0%** (FY25 10.39%, Q2'26 13.10%). Two consecutive quarters below 9% and Pillar 2 is dead; flip to short.
2. **Q3 Power segment EBITDA margin below 17.0%** — the floor of management's own guide, in the quarter the volume ramp lands.
3. **Q3 gas turbine gigawatts below 4.5 GW with HA units ≤4.** Management committed to 5 GW/quarter from Q3'26; ten straight quarters have printed 3–5 GW with nothing above 5.2.
4. **January 2027 call: 2026 equipment backlog margin change below +4 points** (2025 printed +6 points and "at least $8B"). Strazik committed publicly on Sep 16 to disclose it. This is the direct scorecard on Pillar 1.

**The killer question the red teams produced, and the team must be able to answer it on stage:**

> *"At $940 you are paying 21.4 times management's own 2028 EBITDA target. Capitalize a perfectly delivered 2028 at the 25x you say is fair, discount it two years, and you get $877 — below where the stock trades today. That plan needs Power at 22% and Electrification at 22%, and neither segment has ever printed above 18.9% or 18.6% in any quarter, while Wind has had exactly one non-negative quarter in its history. So what am I being paid for the execution risk?"*

**The answer:** nothing on 2028 — which is why our target is +12%, not +25%, and why we are below the Street. What we are paid for is the next twelve months, in which the three arguments that took $256 off this stock each fail again on the record, and a company that has raised its free-cash-flow guidance four consecutive times (FY24 guided $0.7–1.1B → printed $1.70B; FY25 guided $2.0–2.5B → printed $3.71B; FY26 guided $4.5–5.0B → now $11.5–12.5B) publishes the backlog-margin scorecard in January.

---

## 7. The other side's best argument

**Earned free cash flow is approximately zero, and the market is calling it a 4.8% yield.** H1'26 operating cash flow of $10,680M contains a $14,087M increase in customer contract liabilities — so cash from operations *excluding deposits* was **−$3,407M**. FY25 was −$3,363M on the same basis. Since the spin, cumulative FCF of $15.3B sits on a $24.5B deposit build while $7.6B went back to shareholders. Contract liabilities of $40,037M are 3.05x cash on hand and 3.35x book equity. And 40% of the annual bonus plus 50% of the long-term plan pay on this line, with no orders or backlog metric as counterweight.

This survived every attack. It is the question a judge will ask.

**How to handle it in the risk section — do not dodge it.** The deposits are non-refundable (CFO, Oct 22 2025) and are discharged by *delivering turbines at a positive margin*, not by wiring cash back; when the balance stops growing, FCF converges toward EBITDA less capex less tax, not to zero. Roughly $4–5B of the build is already sitting in inventory being manufactured for those same customers. And the short's forward version of this argument contains a confirmed error: it subtracts a twice-raised 2026 guide from an un-raised January cumulative floor. Matched vintages, management's own arithmetic implies ~$7.5B/year for 2027–28 — rising, not collapsing. Concede the quality point; reject the cliff.

---

## 8. What was rejected and why

**Longs.** *Fleet services wave* — 70% of it is just unit growth; the differentiated piece is ~$6/share and lands in 2028. *Deposit engine* — values a customer liability at 100 cents as equity; the market marked the July FCF raise **down** 8.7%. *Backlog conversion* — the model collapses to one input (the 1-year RPO % cancels out), and the same method a year earlier claimed 98% visibility against 66–70% realized. *Vintage rebuttal* — mechanism excellent, but its 44.5% drop-through contradicts its own FY26 build (31.2%) and the 10-K's disclosed 22.5% organic. *Electrification* — compares GEV on 2028E to peers on FY25 actuals; 43% of segment EBITDA cannot offset a Power de-rate. *De-rating mispricing* — capitalizes the price decline itself; the drawdown was a sector move (VRT −25.5%, PWR −11.6%). *Capacity execution* — the 400 installed machines are a company press release; 5.2 GW was already printed in Q2'25. *Demand durability* — defends 2.6% of market cap (next-twelve-months revenue) against a duration problem.

**Shorts.** *Conversion gap* — a denominator artifact; GEV converted 10 GW against Siemens' 12. *Services quality* — divides a net RPO change by GW, ignoring $6.6B of run-off. *Wind bridge* — the miss is real ($480M) but sits inside the guided 12–14% band with ~$560M of cushion; the market paid +13.75% on the worst Wind quarter in two years. *Margin vintage* — dies to POC, and 82% of it was an unsourced multiple assertion. *Multiple compression* — mixes guidance vintages; the "never raised" claim is false ($14B→$22B→$24B in 13 months). *Share loss* — assumes a demand-constrained market in a franchise sold out to 2031. *Cash normalization* — right observation, wrong forward model (liquidation ratio double-counts SRA deposits carrying no RPO). *Shipment stall* — its trigger metric correlates **−0.31** with the revenue line it is supposed to drive.

---

## 9. Open data gaps, in priority order

1. **Firm consensus 2027 adjusted EPS, EBITDA and FCF** (FactSet/Bloomberg). Gating. Every number in Section 4 scales on an assumption nobody verified. Get this before writing a word.
2. **Does GEV bill long-term service agreements on actual or factored fired hours?** Unresolved across four multi-agent runs. It flips the sign on a large part of the $88.5B services RPO debate and therefore on Pillar 3.
3. **Consensus 2027 Power and Electrification segment margins.** Rows 2 and 3 carry most of the model; we are guessing at what the Street carries.
4. **Prolec's clean post-close P&L** — revenue and pre-tax loss are disclosed; EBITDA is not. Our ~$150M purchase-accounting runoff (row 7) is computed from the acquired-intangibles table, not disclosed.
5. **Unit-level HA commercial-operation dates** (McCoy Power Reports or an HA Users Group roster) to replace the fitted fleet cohort with an observed one.
6. **Whether a December 2026 investor update is scheduled.** The Dec 2025 edition printed +15.6% the next day on 3.75x volume and fully reversed within five sessions. If it lands inside the horizon it is the only two-sided catalyst before January.
7. **Short interest, borrow cost and options positioning** — needed for sizing given Oct 28 falls after the finals.

**Two things the team must never put in the memo:** GLJ's vintage argument as a bear risk without the POC rebuttal attached (it dies in one sentence and a judge will know it), and the "+34% equipment revenue step" without the Prolec caveat — 35% of that step is acquisition annualization, not organic growth.
